Hire your first SRE without expecting explicit SRE experience by interviewing for the relevant areas — operations (production insight), software engineering (understanding and improving the software), monitoring systems (measurable SLOs), production automation (scaling operations), and system architecture (scaling the application) — expecting them to occupy an ambiguous position between velocity and reliability that demands resilience and flexibility, and make their initial mission to get up to speed on the service (its current problems, required toil, and the engineering needed to stay within SLOs), doing the engineering to design and implement SLOs and error budgets if the organization lacks them.

Fund SRE from the same source as product development because reliability is a core pillar like testing or security, and keep the supply of SREs smaller than demand — only enough for their specialized work — so you regularly review and prioritize which services receive SRE support, with SRE-to-developer ratios ranging from about 1:5 for low-level infrastructure to about 1:50 for standard-framework consumer apps and often around 1:10.
Treat SRE as a global community of practitioners extending far beyond Google (of which Google is just one member) and treat DevOps and SRE as complementary rather than at odds.

Recognize for operational decisions: SRE work applies computer science and software engineering to large distributed systems, including service code, reusable operational infrastructure, and adaptation of existing solutions to new reliability problems.

SREs doing software development should keep working as SREs rather than becoming full-time embedded developers, so they retain the production perspective of being both creator and customer of the product.

Do not lower standards for internally-developed SRE software: apply the same code review, integration and end-to-end testing, and production-readiness review you would require to onboard any other team's service.

In a major migration, let SRE drive the infrastructure design (their domain of extracting and processing data at scale) while developers own the business logic, define the interfaces between them early so each team works independently, sync where they interact, validate the new system by requiring its output to match the old system's exactly, and stand up a production-like test environment to measure performance while business logic is still being developed.

Scale reliability best by providing product-development teams a platform of SRE-validated, reliable, and scalable infrastructure, which removes classes of cognitive load and lets developers focus innovation at the application layer.
Have SREs work as part of the development team — with highly visible, reviewed work — rather than as an external unit, to ensure effective knowledge sharing.

Involve SRE in the design phase to prevent incidents — the best production incidents are those that never happen — and so that SRE shares ownership of any deliberately less-than-ideal trade-offs, minimizing future disputes once the service is in production.

Frameworks give universal support by design: services that cannot warrant full SRE engagement can still use SRE-developed production features, which breaks the SRE staffing barrier, raises baseline service quality, and lets every framework-built service automatically inherit later improvements to the framework.

A common production platform enables a shared-responsibility model in which SREs own and maintain the platform infrastructure — control systems such as load shedding, overload protection, automation, traffic management, logging, and monitoring — while development teams stay on-call for functional bugs in their application code.

Prioritize organizational culture over tooling, have all roles minding a service use the same tools, and value API-oriented system management over any particular toolset, since divergent tooling reduces the benefit of every improvement and a specific tool will be outlasted by the philosophy.
Use objective measurement to establish the reality of what is happening, verify that changes have the expected effect, and create a shared, objective basis that different functions can agree upon.
Minimize toil and cap the time a team member spends on it at about 50%, treating the cap as a guarantee of engineering time; if a machine can perform an operation, a machine often should.
Use the wisdom of production — real-time feedback on how a system actually behaves — to inform better system design, rather than relying on a whiteboarded view isolated from the facts on the ground.

Do not tie incentives to a single narrow numeric measure, which will be gamed (Goodhart's law); remove incentives to pass blame between groups, give people freedom to find the right tradeoffs, and hold SRE roles in the same esteem and pay as their product-development peers.
Engage SRE early, ideally at design time, because a system designed with early SRE engagement typically works better in production regardless of who later operates it.

Engage SRE across the whole service lifecycle (engagement can begin at any stage, and applying production knowledge can substantially improve reliability well before any SRE picks up the pager): in architecture and design, create best practices such as resilience to single points of failure, document infrastructure dos and don'ts from prior experience, provide early-engagement consulting, and codesign the service, because fixing architectural mistakes becomes harder later and early engagement avoids costly redesigns that become necessary when systems meet real users and must scale.

For a full-time SRE engagement, prefer embedding an SRE within the product-development team to provide focus and give both sides maximum time to learn from each other as developers ramp up on SRE skills, reserve part-time engagement for fairly brief constrained projects, and gauge the team's or application's maturity relative to SRE practices when scoping.

Set clear shared expectations for an SRE engagement: application owners (not SREs) are directly responsible for changes to the application, SRE engagement should improve company-wide common tools rather than produce one-off scripts, SREs are not traditional operations engineers and do not support manual work like running a deployment job, and SRE must give the developer team a heads-up about any new processes it introduces such as load testing.

When spinning up two sister teams, choose among models — both halves starting at the same time, setting up the developer-colocated site first so SREs engage earlier in the product lifecycle, or setting up the non-colocated site first (or sharing the pager) for a service already in production — according to where the right people are at the right time.
Treat as operational guidance: SRE's role in product launches is to enable a rapid pace of change without compromising the stability of the site.

Give new SREs targeted project work with partial ownership rather than menial work, splitting their time between learning and projects, with starter projects such as shipping a small feature, adding monitoring to a blind spot, or automating a pain point to build empathy and an appreciation for removing toil.

Hold a regular production meeting with compulsory SRE attendance plus major stakeholders and partner product-development teams, to preserve the operations feedback loop, and treat an inability to invite your dev partners as a relationship to be fixed.

Collaborate between product development and SRE as early as the design phase, before any code is committed, because SRE recommendations about architecture and software behavior are difficult or impossible to retrofit later.

Engage SRE as early as the design phase, because the earlier the engagement the lower the cost to onboard and the more reliable the service is out of the gate, since you avoid spending time unwinding suboptimal design and implementation.
Treat SLO violations as blameless triggers that bring stakeholder teams back to the drawing board, since the SLO was a collaborative decision among them.

Adopt an error-budget-based approach only when its four preconditions hold — SLOs approved by all stakeholders, agreement they are achievable under normal circumstances, an organizational commitment formalized in an error budget policy to use the budget for decisions, and a process for refining the SLO — otherwise SLO compliance is merely another KPI rather than a decision-making tool.

Express each SLI as the ratio of good events to total events on a 0-100% scale, define the error budget as 100% minus the SLO, and make all SLIs follow a consistent numerator/denominator/threshold style so alerting, analysis, error-budget calculation, and reporting tools can share the same inputs.

Get explicit agreement from all stakeholders before relying on an SLO — product managers accept the threshold as good enough, developers commit to reducing risk when the budget is exhausted, and the production team agrees it is defensible without Herculean effort, excessive toil, or burnout — and defend it with monitoring and alerting that warn of threats to the error budget before they become deficits.

Derive an error budget from the SLO and write a policy specifying the actions to take and who takes them when the budget is exhausted; getting that policy approved by the product manager, developers, and SREs tests whether the SLO is fit for purpose, and everyone must understand that lowering the SLO also lowers the number of situations to which SREs respond.

Use established error-budget-exhaustion actions: have the development team give top priority to reliability bugs, focus exclusively on reliability until the system is within SLO (with approval to push back on external feature requests), and apply a production freeze that halts risky changes until budget is restored.

Document the SLO prominently with its authors, reviewers, approvers, approval and next-review dates, service description, objectives and SLI implementations, error-budget calculation, and rationale (recording even that an SLO is ad hoc), review it at a cadence matched to your SLO maturity, and include in the policy a clear escalation path for disagreements about the calculation or the actions.

Maintain dashboards and reports showing in-time SLO compliance and SLI trends so you can communicate status and detect a higher-than-usual budget-burn rate, and use error-budget consumption to quantify and rank incidents and identify the ones meriting closer investigation.

Define a documented error-budget policy that says what happens when the SLO is missed (including a change freeze) and what happens when a dependency causes the miss; a freeze regardless of cause keeps users happier, but record the practical decision for your service in advance.

Use the error-budget/SLO model as a shared, fact-based language that removes subjectivity so ops and dev reach the same decision from the same data, embracing the differences between the disciplines rather than converting one into the other.

Agree principles of cooperation up front and establish the SLO from the start rather than backtracking to it later: a definition of and hard limit on operational work, a measured SLO used to prioritize engineering work for both teams, a quarterly error budget determining release velocity and safety parameters, and developer involvement in daily operations so ongoing issues stay visible.

Structure an SLO document with metadata (status, author, reviewers, approvers, approval date, and revisit date), a service overview, a precise definition of each SLI including its exact measurement formula and SLO target, a rationale, and a clarifications-and-caveats section, documenting when the numbers are not strongly evidence-based so future readers understand it and can decide whether collecting more evidence is worth the investment, and give each SLO objective a separate error budget defined as 100% minus that objective's goal, enacting the error budget policy when any one objective has exhausted its budget.

Frame the error budget policy's goals as protecting customers from repeated SLO misses and incentivizing a balance of reliability against other features — not as punishment for missing SLOs — giving teams permission to focus exclusively on reliability when the data indicates reliability matters more than other product features.

Under a typical SLO-miss policy, let releases proceed per the release policy while the service is at or above its SLO, but when the service has exceeded its error budget over the preceding window, halt all changes and releases other than the highest-priority issues or security fixes until it is back within SLO.

Have the error budget policy distinguish when a team must work on reliability — a code bug or procedural error caused the miss, a postmortem reveals an opportunity to soften a hard dependency, or miscategorized errors hid budget consumption that would have caused a miss — from when it may continue feature work, such as an outage from a company-wide networking problem, one caused by another team that has itself frozen releases, or budget consumed by users out of scope for the SLO like load tests or penetration testers.
Define a quarterly error budget from the service's SLO so both SRE and product development share an objective metric for how unreliable the service may be, removing politics from risk negotiation.

Distinguish a service level agreement from an SLO: an SLA is a business contract that triggers compensation when users are unhappy enough, whereas the SLO is the internal reliability target you manage to.

Recognize for operational decisions: Distinguish three terms precisely: an SLI is a quantitative measure of a service level, an SLO is a target value or range for an SLI, and an SLA is a contract with explicit consequences for meeting or missing SLOs.
Write a service level objective first if one does not exist, because the SLO is the single most important lever for moving a team from reactive ops work to a healthy, long-term SRE focus.

Separate the SLI specification (the user-relevant outcome, independent of measurement) from its implementation (the specification plus a way to measure it), recognizing that one specification can have several implementations differing in quality, coverage, and cost.

Choose a small number of SLI types (five or fewer) representing the most critical customer functionality, and start by picking relevant but easy-to-measure aspects: one application, a clear definition of who the users are, the common user interactions, and a high-level architecture diagram of components, request flow, data flow, and critical dependencies.

Abstract a system into a few component types and pick the SLI types relevant to each: availability, latency, and quality for request-driven components; freshness, correctness, and coverage for pipelines; and durability for storage.

For a first SLI implementation pick the option requiring the least engineering work (such as existing server logs), but when a closer-to-the-user option is already available prefer it (for example load-balancer monitoring over application-server logs), and ensure any curated test data behind a correctness SLI is representative of real-world data.

Do not wait for a perfect first SLI or SLO: get something measured and set up a feedback loop to improve it, and avoid setting an SLO purely from current performance, which can lock in unnecessarily strict targets.
Use multiple SLO thresholds (grades) for an SLI to capture both the typical experience and the long tail, for example 90% of requests faster than 100 ms and 99% faster than 400 ms.

Continuously improve SLO targets: gather a cheap source of user-satisfaction information and iterate from it, validate the SLO by correlating outages and ticket spikes with error-budget drops, treat coverage gaps as normal and refine SLIs and SLOs over time, and when tightening an SLO balance recall against precision so the team is not flooded with unimportant events.

Improve an SLI implementation by moving the measurement closer to the user or by improving coverage, use an aspirational SLO (tracked alongside the current one but marked as not requiring action) when a tighter target is needed but not yet achievable, and pick the highest-ROI iteration, erring toward quicker and cheaper metrics first.

Run a periodic SLO review cycle that avoids both over-frequent changes and staleness — for example a six-month SLO revision cycle plus a monthly SLO performance review producing action items to restore the service to SLO or adjust an unrealistic target.
Do not require SLOs to be met 100% of the time; instead allow an error budget — a permitted rate of SLO misses — and track it on a daily or weekly basis.

Choose the SLO time window deliberately — rolling windows track user experience and calendar windows track business planning, defining rolling windows as an integral number of weeks — and use a four-week rolling window as a good general-purpose interval, complemented by weekly summaries for task prioritization and quarterly reports for project planning.
Count planned maintenance windows as downtime in SLO calculations, because uninformed users experience them as generic unexplained downtime.

Write SLOs in terms of user-centric actions using critical user journeys (sequences of core tasks essential to a user's experience), which improves recall without affecting precision, and grade interaction importance with bucketing — adding labels to SLIs and applying different SLOs per label, such as by customer tier or expected responsiveness.

Require a critical dependency's reliability guarantee to be at least as high as the reliability of the action that depends on it (owned by the team running it), and engineer around a component with inherent reliability limits below what its dependent journey needs by using a different component or adding defenses such as caching, offline store-and-forward processing, or graceful degradation.

Reliability engineering should account for the full lifecycle of a service, including design, deployment, operation, refinement, and decommissioning, because a large share of system cost occurs after initial release.
Teams should invest in reliability improvements only until the service is reliable enough, then shift effort toward features or new products.
Small organizations should put lightweight reliability support in place early because expanding an existing reliability structure is less costly than introducing one after it is absent.
Recognize for operational decisions: Beyond a certain scale a system must be self-repairing, because a large number of component failures is statistically guaranteed to occur every second.
Treat as operational guidance: Reliability is the fundamental feature of a system, and autonomous, resilient behavior is one effective way to achieve it.

Do not naively multiply per-instance failure probabilities to claim redundancy gains: instances across zones share dependencies, failure domains, and global control planes, so only count redundancy you can justify after enumerating every shared dependency and failure pattern.

Only deliberately relax reliability (e.g. inject latency) to measure user impact when you are confident there is error budget to burn, cross that line thoughtfully, and beware that zero measured conversion loss may just mean users have no alternative rather than that reliability does not matter.

Measure availability with a status endpoint that exercises most of the stack and returns 200 when healthy, polled by an external prober independent of your environment, and require a second geographically separate prober to confirm before marking a node down to avoid false positives.

Do not wall yourself off from your cloud or dependency providers: share your SLO and real-time performance so both work from the same dashboards, because a provider's global SLO can read green while your small slice is far worse.

Do not set SLOs on infrastructure utilization, because users only care that traffic is handled and the service is up, fast, and error-free; keep monitoring utilization and doing capacity planning, but outside the SLO framework.

Use SLOs to engage your cloud provider's reliability engineers — for example having them paged alongside your own for SLO-impacting events — to triage root causes hidden behind cloud abstraction and reduce mean time to repair.

Agree in advance with partners that when shared-SLO impact is high enough both sides escalate to P1 with special handling such as a shared bridge, even when the normal ticket model would rank the issue lower.

Build an SLO culture deliberately across people, process, and technology: a common vernacular, evangelism (training, early adopters, a memorable acronym), automation that auto-collects SLIs, and incentives such as manager goals — and expect it to take patience and years, implemented piece by piece.

Adopt SLOs even without automated SLI collection — automation accelerates adoption but is not a prerequisite, and there is real benefit to just writing SLOs — and have the business owner (often the product manager) set each SLO from business criticality, expressed in business terms.

Base the SLO framework on the small consistent signal set services already monitor — volume, availability, latency, errors, and tickets (VALET, aligned with the Four Golden Signals) — and standardize their naming and measurement across services.

In a dynamic cloud environment of live migrations and variable latency, monitor at a higher level using user-facing indicators (such as API responsiveness) rather than low-level infrastructure signals, and reframe paging in terms of explicit first-principle SLOs to trim monitoring fat and avoid chasing transient problems.
The four golden signals for a user-facing system are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation; if you can measure only four metrics, measure these.

Use percentiles (at least 90th, preferably 95th/99th for user-facing services) rather than arithmetic averages for latency SLOs, and require the monitoring system to compute those percentiles, because the mean masks whether 1%, 5%, or 50% of requests are slow.
Treat most metrics as distributions rather than averages, because a simple average obscures long-tail behavior such as a slow tail of requests.

Standardize error semantics: never signal an error in a 2xx body, return 5xx for service-caused and 4xx for client-caused errors, track both but set SLOs only on 5xx, and keep the definition generic enough that batch services map errors to failed records.

Choose monitoring that meets predetermined freshness and retention needs: data more than four to five minutes stale impairs incident response, retain detailed metrics multi-month for trend analysis and 'has this happened before?', and record event/resource metrics as monotonic counters so windowed rates can be computed.

Treat metrics and structured logging as the two primary monitoring data sources for distinct jobs: use near-real-time metrics for alerting and dashboards (even for single rare events, by incrementing a counter and alerting on it) and use more granular but delayed logs for root-cause analysis and detailed reports.

Promote important low-cardinality log signals (such as HTTP status code) into metric labels to enable per-category graphing and accurate per-category alert thresholds without exploding metric volume, and tailor dashboards consistently to each audience.

Build pipelines from reusable code libraries and a microservice structure: add a monitoring metric once and share it across pipelines/stages (e.g. a generic data-freshness alert for many jobs), and prefer many small pipelines that each do one task well, share core libraries, vary only in business logic, and can be released and monitored separately, over one monolith.
Collect centralized events, logs, and metrics across business logic, applications, infrastructure, and customer-impact periods.

Monitor production for real-time business intelligence, immediate incident response, and capacity planning, building the strategy on four areas: instrumenting applications and infrastructure, storing the data, creating aggregating dashboards, and setting up notifications.

Gather monitoring data from hardware, operating system, middleware, and applications, instrument applications with hooks for what operations and business users care about plus version reporting, set log levels by recoverability, and treat logging as first-level requirements in a single-line, grep-able format.

Make alert response proportional: classify alerts into severity levels (ticket a low error rate lasting over an hour, treat a 100% error rate as an immediate emergency) and suppress redundant alerts — alert once on a global rate, suppress a service alert when its dependency is already alerting — but ensure suppression lifts once the event ends.

Tie alerts directly to SLOs through a uniform control surface that decides at request time whether an error is user-impacting and writes that decision to both logs and metrics, making alerts clearly actionable and lowering false positives.

Never use a high-cardinality value (millions of possible values, such as an entity ID) as a metric label; keep it in logs and embed the one-off log query in the alert so responders can run it quickly.

Choose a load metric that captures the real burden (the number of pages was insufficient; a better metric measured how much time an on-caller needed to resolve a ticket after their shift ended), and relieve alert-driven overload by auditing and removing alerts that do not represent user-facing problems and silencing alerts generously — each only for a limited period (typically a day, up to a week) so it does not mask outages, assigning any alert not fixable within a few minutes to a tracking ticket — rather than trying to find the source of every alert at once.

Before adding an alert rule, confirm it detects an otherwise-undetected condition that is urgent, actionable, and actively or imminently user-visible, and that you cannot safely ignore or automate it.
Group multiple alerts triggered by the same event into a single incident, so you can analyze incidents per day separately from alerts per day and avoid duplicated debugging or panic.

Put SLI metrics prominently on the service dashboard (ideally the landing page) as the first thing to check when an SLO alert fires, and add monitoring of intended changes — binary version, flags, and config version — surfaced in alert-linked dashboards to correlate outages with rollouts.

Design alerting metrics to change dramatically only when the system enters a problem state and stay steady in normal operation, while debugging metrics instead point at the suspect aspect of the system; after each postmortem add the metrics that would have diagnosed the issue faster.

Frame SLO-based alerting as detecting events that consume a large fraction of the error budget (across all SLIs, not just ones named 'error'), and evaluate any alerting strategy simultaneously on precision, recall, detection time, and reset time.

Do not use a duration ('for') clause as SLO alerting criteria: it does not scale with severity (a 100% outage alerts no faster than a 0.2% one) and resets if the SLI momentarily recovers, so a fluctuating SLI may never alert.

Keep alerting scalable and low-toil: decide window and burn-rate parameters once and apply them to all services rather than per-service, and manage many SLOs by grouping request types into a few availability buckets (e.g. CRITICAL, HIGH_FAST, HIGH_SLOW, LOW, NO_SLO) instead of unique objectives per request type.

Configure alerting from meaningful, metric-represented SLOs to notify on-call only on actionable, specific error-budget threats, using multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerting as the default technique for defending an application's SLOs.

Design a pipeline resilient enough that a machine or zonal outage never triggers an SLO-violation page (by the time you are paged, automated measures are exhausted and you must intervene manually), so that with well-defined SLOs and reliable detection you are alerted before customers notice, and respond quickly with proactive customer communication when an SLO is violated.

Because SLO-violation monitoring only alerts after customers are affected, add sufficient operational monitoring (starting with basic metrics like CPU and building to more complex ones) to resolve or mitigate issues before an SLO breaks, and gather only the right amount of logging — rate-limit or log only interesting requests such as those raising unhandled exceptions, since logging every request of a high-volume component drowns useful logs, fills disk, and degrades performance, treating reading production logs as a last resort.

Get your customers to measure SLIs and alert on SLOs and share those measurements with you, because absent a stated SLO a customer will invent one and not tell you until you fail it: sit down to explain SLOs, SLIs, and error budgets, help them describe their critical applications in those terms, audit their monitoring to turn off alerting with zero SLO impact (often up to half of what they measure), assemble the remaining useful measurements into their SLOs, cover uncovered SLO dimensions, and build shared SLO dashboards so neither side has to swap extra information when an SLO is threatened.

Improving reliability over time requires starting from a known baseline and tracking progress, so passively collect all alerts in an outage-tracking tool that lets you annotate, group, and analyze them.

Make monitoring aware of all release versions on both sides of a service interface, run cross-version compatibility tests whenever either side cuts a release, and have rollout automation block a rollout until problematic version combinations are no longer possible.

Monitor direct dependencies (request/response size, latency, response codes per the four golden signals) by instrumenting the shared lower-level RPC client library once rather than each client, so new dependencies are monitored for free.

Monitor saturation of every resource the service relies on — hard limits (RAM, disk, CPU quota) and soft ones (file descriptors, thread pools, queue wait, log volume, language runtime resources) — alert as a resource nears a hard limit or degradation threshold, and track all of them for capacity planning.

Break served traffic down by status code (monitor all HTTP response codes even those too noisy to alert on, plus quota/rate-limit denials) and design every exposed metric around a concrete use — capacity planning, debugging, or notification — rather than exporting metrics just because they are easy.

Prefer scenario-based, composable capacity tests over isolated benchmarks, set pass thresholds by ratcheting above a minimum, base load calculations on peak load, and isolate the capacity environment, avoiding virtualization unless production is virtual.

Do not alert simply when a short-window error rate exceeds the SLO threshold (good recall and detection but poor precision — up to 144 alerts/day while still meeting SLO), and do not lengthen the window naively, since longer windows worsen reset time and cost more memory and I/O.

Alert on error-budget burn rate (rate 1 exactly exhausts the budget over the window) to get good detection time and high precision from a smaller, cheaper window, and use multiple burn-rate alerts at different windows to catch both fast spikes and slow sustained burns.

Make every paging alert immediately actionable (requiring a human to do something the system cannot) with a high signal-to-noise ratio and few false positives to avoid alert fatigue, and for a team committed to SLO- and symptom-based alerting, recognize that relaxing alert thresholds is rarely an appropriate response to being paged.

As starting points, page on 2% budget consumed in 1 hour and 5% in 6 hours, ticket on 10% in 3 days, send pages for budget-exhausting-in-hours issues and tickets for slower ones (pages and tickets being the only valid ways to summon a human), and tune the numbers to the service's baseline load.

Prefer multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerting: require a shorter window (about one-twelfth of the long window) to also be over threshold so the alert fires only while budget is actively burning, and add suppression so simultaneously-true burn-rate conditions do not fire multiple notifications for one incident.

Recognize that burn-rate alerting over-pages low-traffic services (one failure in ten requests is a 10% error rate, a 1,000x burn against 99.9%) and handle them by generating artificial traffic, combining related services that share a failure domain, or changing the product so a single failure carries less weight or takes more requests to qualify.

Tune alerting parameters to the availability target's extremes: a very low target (e.g. 90%) may never fire a budget-percentage alert on a 100% outage, while a very high target (99.999% burns out in ~26s) cannot be defended by alerting and must instead be engineered so a full outage is extremely unlikely — for example rolling changes to only 1% of users to burn budget at 1% of the rate.
Alert on a computed ratio such as error rate divided by request rate combined with an absolute floor on the count, so that tiny absolute numbers of errors do not trigger a page.

Reduce the impact of a single failed request with client retries using exponential backoff and jitter plus fallback paths that capture requests for later execution, which allows more failed events in the budget, more monitoring signal, and more response time — and if small budget losses do not noticeably affect users, consider lowering the SLO or widening the window (a product decision tied to the error-budget policy).

Guard against the classic cascading failure where a surge makes overloaded backends slow rather than refusing requests, requests time out to the load balancer, retries pile on more load, and frontend capacity collapses — by giving clients jitter and truncated exponential backoff to avoid a synchronized thundering-herd of retries.

Use canarying to minimize SLO and error-budget risk, since budget impact is proportional to traffic exposed to defects (a 5% canary of a candidate failing 20% of requests yields only a 1% overall error rate versus 20% globally), and keep the canary risk model the simplest that meets your technical and business objectives, because chasing technical correctness leads to overinvestment and incessant tuning for no real benefit — all models are wrong, but some are useful.

Avoid overachieving your SLO, because users build on your actual performance; deliberately reduce over-delivery via planned outages, request throttling, or not being faster under light load to prevent hidden over-dependence.

Limit retries with both a per-request retry budget (for example, three attempts) and a per-client retry budget that allows retries only while retries stay below about 10% of requests, which reduces retry-induced amplification from roughly 3x to about 1.1x.

Limit retries per request and add a server-wide retry budget (for example, 60 retries per minute per process) that fails fast once exceeded, to contain a local capacity failure from escalating into a global cascading failure.

Identify and attack toil — repetitive, automatable, reactive work of no enduring value that grows with the service and deflates morale — by rewarding root-cause fixes over symptom-masking workarounds and using an objective cost figure (such as dollars per hour of a recurring problem) to convince the owning team to fix the root cause.

When a team is in toil overload, treat reduction as its own data-driven project: track toil in ranked bugs by fix-cost and time-saved, consider outright rejecting a toil-intensive task after a cost analysis, and intentionally batch or delay toil so it accumulates for parallel processing and reveals patterns to target.

Measure toil objectively rather than by intuition, in three steps — identify it (with the people who do the work), pick a consistent unit of human effort (minutes, tickets, manual changes, including context-switching cost), and track it continuously before/during/after reduction — keeping the measurement itself lightweight so it does not create toil.

Before a toil-reduction project, weigh cost versus benefit and confirm time saved is at least proportional to time invested, but still pursue projects that look unprofitable on hours alone when they yield indirect benefits such as morale, fewer human-error outages, security, or career growth.

Recognize that eliminating toil is not always the right move: once identified, decide whether reduction makes sense using metrics, ROI analysis, risk assessment, and iterative development — then be relentless, since benefits usually exceed costs even if you start with only a small proof of concept.

Focus troubleshooting on novel failure modes, not the same brittle failure every week, and account for dependency math: each new critical dependency of availability P reduces overall availability by 1−P, so a four-nines service with nine critical four-nines dependencies degrades to three nines.

Automate incrementally toward self-service: start complex, edge-heavy problems with a human-backed typed interface ('engineer behind the curtain'), then expose self-service methods (form, script, API, documented PR) that gracefully degrade to a ticket, since moving 80–90% of requests to self-service is a huge workload reduction even with some one-offs remaining.
Use tickets as a quick-and-dirty GUI and fallback for automation — logging work, updating stakeholders, and routing requests the automation cannot handle to a manual queue.

Make lifecycle and turnup automation owned by the team that owns the service, exposed as a service (e.g., an Admin Server with fine-grained ACLs) behind a stable API contract, so the implementation can change without breaking callers.

Secure management and colleague support for toil reduction backed by objective metrics, accepting reduced short-term feature capacity for long-term team health, and strengthen the business case by coupling the reduction with another desirable goal such as security, scalability, or reliability so users willingly give up toil-generating systems.

Do not chase a perfect toil-eliminating system in one step: automate a few high-priority items first, reinvest the time gained to improve the solution, and measure success with a clear metric such as Mean Time to Repair.

Increase production uniformity with a 'pets versus cattle' approach — give many devices the same interface so they are interchangeable and need less maintenance — accepting high initial cost for lower medium-to-long-term maintenance, disaster-recovery, and utilization cost, and let teams keep their own tools only if they own the toil from unsupported or legacy choices.

Mitigate faster by promptly rolling back a recent code or config rollout that introduced a bug, generally preferring 'roll back, fix, roll forward' over 'roll forward, fix, roll forward again' since even a quick fix must be tested/built/rolled out — and rolling back usually impacts users far less, because a roll-forward build can exceed a tight error budget (99.99% affords only ~15 minutes per quarter).

Preserve the ability to mitigate: avoid changes that cannot be rolled back (API-incompatible changes, lockstep releases) wherever possible, and use feature isolation so a misbehaving feature can be disabled via a feature flag without affecting others — which also improves release velocity and simplifies the decision to disable it.

Drain requests away from system elements exhibiting a bug — such as the portion of a gradual rollout that got a bad update — to mitigate customer impact in seconds rather than the minutes a rollback may take.

During an incident, prioritize mitigating damage and returning the system to a stable previous state and refrain from deploying major changes, the exception being an immediate rollback when recently deployed code is the cause.
Recognize for operational decisions: Reliable processes tend to increase developer agility, because rapid, reliable rollouts make production changes easier to see and bugs faster to find and fix.
Test rollback procedures in a test environment before running large-scale tests, because untested rollback procedures are often flawed and lengthen outages.

Prefer tests that catch a bug with zero mean-time-to-repair by blocking the push so the bug never reaches production, because the more zero-MTTR bugs you catch, the higher the mean time between failures your users experience.

Aim to identify the root cause of every page — root causes extend into team processes, so a bug a unit test would have caught is really a process bug — and rarely conclude 'cause unknown', because explaining a page away as transient invites recurrence onto the next on-call engineer.

Limit on-call shifts to 12 hours because long shifts cause exhaustion and tired people make mistakes; a 12-hour system needs no globally distributed team, since even a single site can split day and overnight shifts between two engineers rather than running unsustainable 24-hour shifts.

Make part-time and reduced-hours work compatible with on-call: configure the scheduler to skip non-working days, split shifts for engineers on reduced daily hours, and give reduced-hours engineers a proportionately smaller on-call share.

Staff sister SRE teams on different continents for service reliability (one continues if a disaster stops the other), reduced on-call stress (12-hour shifts), broader recruiting (shifts overlapping the normal working day), and improved production maturity, colocating each SRE team with its development team where possible (separation makes it harder for SREs to understand how services evolve and for developers to value infrastructure improvements), and when choosing locations balance the mutually exclusive objectives of minimizing out-of-normal-hours on-call against maximizing online overlap — six to eight time zones apart works well and avoids midnight-to-6 a.m. shifts, seeding the first team in a new office with SREs willing to relocate and a high-value project requiring interaction with the sister team.

Treat on-call rotation design as a matter of flexibility, not fixed rules, because team members' needs change and a fair, equitable balance of on-call and personal life requires accommodating diverse needs.

Size on-call teams to absorb a temporary staff reduction without overloading the rest: a sustainable 24/7 rotation needs at minimum five engineers per site multisite or eight single-site, plus one extra per site as protection (six per site multisite, nine single-site).

Invest in on-call team relationships — offsites, having the whole rotation sit and eat together regardless of title — because stronger bonds create an 'I protect my colleagues' mentality that makes engineers more likely to fix bugs, finish action items, and avoid carelessly paging teammates.

Strengthen management presence against overload: recognize that a manager not on the on-call rotation does not directly feel the team's stress and a team that is not heard feels distant from management, so assign a dedicated manager who is not shared across multiple teams and uses a participatory management style, and give members more control and power (resisting the temptation to micromanage under stress, keeping the team in the loop, and prioritizing together) to reduce perceived overload and increase performance and job satisfaction.

Automate on-call scheduling with a tool that rebalances shifts as needs change, factors in preferences and recent load for fairness (not perfect uniformity), and never alters an already-generated schedule so engineers can plan around it, supported by a documented swap policy with peer review and commute coverage where a strict pager-response SLO applies.

Distinguish resolving an incident (mitigating impact and restoring service) from managing it (coordinating responding teams and ensuring communication flows among responders and to stakeholders), and respond in a structured way agreed beforehand so the team concentrates on resolution rather than process when disaster strikes.

Apply the basic incident-response principles — maintain a clear line of command, designate clearly defined roles, keep a working record of debugging and mitigation as you go, and declare incidents early and often — to satisfy the three Cs (Coordinate, Communicate, Control), since incident-response failures usually trace to one of those three.

Organize incident response into three roles — Incident Commander (leads/coordinates and assumes any undelegated role), Operations Lead (applies operational tools to mitigate and resolve), and Communications Lead (public face giving periodic stakeholder updates) — with the person who declares the incident typically becoming the Incident Commander.

Put a formal incident-response structure in place early to prevent uncoordinated parallel investigations, with the Incident Commander proactively coordinating information and making decisions rather than merely relaying messages, and assigned to the team with the best visibility into customer impact while delegating well-understood problems to the Operations Lead.

Separate incident-response responsibilities into distinct roles and have each person stay within their role, because a clear separation of responsibilities paradoxically gives responders more autonomy by removing the need to second-guess colleagues.
Perform rollouts only during business days and hours so developers are reachable if something goes wrong, rather than on weekends when they are not.

Do not rely on heroics from individuals tapped during their free time — if they had been unreachable the response would have failed — so provide coverage through an on-call rotation with paid out-of-hours coverage instead.

Stop the impact first, then find the root cause unless it surfaces early, and after a successful mitigation postpone any risky rollout until the root cause is fully determined rather than continuing and risking a larger disruption.

Develop generic mitigations ahead of time — blunt actions first responders can apply quickly to stop the bleeding before the root cause is understood, such as rolling back a correlated release or reconfiguring load balancers away from an affected region — recognizing you only need to know the location of the root cause, not full details, to mitigate, and build general-purpose mitigation tools (like rollback tooling) before an incident, mining past postmortems for tools that would have helped.

Prioritize mitigation above all else during an active incident, because customers want the errors to stop rather than a full understanding of the cause, and address the incident in order: assess impact, mitigate impact, perform root-cause analysis, then after it ends fix the cause, write a postmortem, and run incident-response drills against the exercised vulnerabilities.

Declare incidents early and often because managed incidents resolve faster: early declaration prevents cross-team miscommunication, brings root-cause identification and resolution sooner, and loops in relevant teams earlier for faster external communication.
Early in an incident, quickly verify it is affecting actual customers and use a pre-prepared incident-management system to bring in a communications person who informs customers of the outage.

Equip incident response with the right tools and preparation before any incident: keep on-call info, service ownership, postmortems, and incident metadata in one system to assemble the team fast; use a dedicated chat channel as the scribe's ledger of actions, owners, and timestamps; make coordination decisions on a recorded conference call with outcomes logged in chat so any timeline can be reconstructed.

Decide and rehearse the single incident communication channel beforehand (preferably a familiar one) so the Incident Commander never chooses it mid-incident, prepare two or three ready-to-use public-announcement templates with a known send path and an agreed draft/review/approve/release flow, prepare distribution lists for an 'all hands on deck' call, and establish explicit criteria — derived from past outages and high-risk areas — for when an issue is truly an incident.
Base incident management on a recognized, scalable structure such as the Incident Command System, known for its clarity and scalability.

Hand over incident command — including across a shift boundary — to the more experienced or available commander as soon as coordination and communication become a challenge, rather than waiting for the normal handover time, and rotate on-call engineers and the Incident Commander periodically (e.g. every four hours) during long incidents to encourage rest and bring fresh ideas.

When a problem is vague and uncovered by existing procedures, have the Incident Commander assign a dedicated owner to coordinate it, monitor progress closely, and organize more engineers when new tools must be written quickly.
Assign an Incident Commander who holds the high-level state of the incident, structures the response, assigns responsibilities, and by default holds every role they have not delegated.

Declare an incident early and close it out if the fix turns out to be simple, rather than spinning up the framework hours into a growing problem, and set clear declaration conditions such as needing a second team, customer-visible impact, or being unsolved after an hour of focused analysis.

Make the Communications Lead report accurate information tailored to each audience — leaders need extent and progress assurance, dependent teams need recovery timelines, external customers need proactive notification, and ticket-filers need workarounds and timelines — and keep the audience informed with regular status updates, since silence makes people assume nothing is being done and a missing all-clear makes them assume the incident continues.
Treat incident-response processes as purposefully non-static: review and update them periodically (e.g. every few months) to reflect changing business needs as the organization grows.

Practice incident teamwork with regular failure-injection exercises using the same processes and vernacular as a real incident (a trainee acting as Incident Commander), supplemented by time-bound simulation games that capture the urgency real drills cannot, and make training hands-on by analyzing past incidents.

Practice incident management with regular drills — controlled customer-safe emergencies (company-wide disaster-recovery testing), Wheel-of-Misfortune role-plays, or deliberately escalating a minor problem — using real tools as much as possible, follow each with a report of what went well, poorly, and how to improve, and establish and rehearse procedures while the world is not on fire to build the muscle memory to stay calm, securing leadership support for dedicated practice time.

Use the incident-management framework routinely — for cross-team change management, disaster-recovery testing, and role-play of past incidents — because incident-management proficiency atrophies quickly when not exercised.

Adopt a blameless postmortem culture as a cultural as much as technical change: start small with a basic procedure then reflect and tune it to your organization (no one size fits all), because well-written, acted-upon, widely-shared postmortems drive positive change and prevent repeat outages, with action items measurably reducing the blast radius and rate of similar future incidents.

Keep postmortems blameless by attributing failure to systemic and process causes (e.g. nothing stopped a human from running unsafe automation and no documentation warned of the gotcha) rather than an individual's 'careless ignorance', focusing the root-cause section on what went wrong not who, and aiming action items at improving the system rather than improving people.

Write postmortem action items that prevent as well as mitigate, preferring fixes to automated systems and processes over changing human behavior (humans stay fallible), assign each a priority and an owner with precise, measurable, verifiable language (avoid vague 'improve'/'make better'), file a tracking bug for every one, and group action items by theme for large incidents to ease assigning owners and priorities.

Keep postmortems blameless and factual: avoid finger-pointing (which makes people risk-averse and prone to covering up critical facts), strip personal judgments, dramatic or animated wording (justify any severity with verifiable data), use non-leading language that does not put recipients on the defensive, and redirect even senior-leader blame into generic questions like 'were there warning signs we could have heeded, and why did we dismiss them?'.

Give each postmortem a single accountable owner (point of contact for the document, follow-up, and completion) with multiple collaborators including all incident participants, since writing in isolation overlooks contributing factors and unowned action items go unresolved.

Sustain a healthy postmortem culture from the top: senior leadership must support, exemplify, and enforce blameless behavior in every discussion, reward closing action items (not just writing the document) to avoid an unvirtuous cycle of unclosed postmortems, and incentivize the change postmortems drive via peer bonuses, performance reviews, promotion, recognizing owners as experts, and gamifying closure with scoreboards, burndowns, or FixIt weeks.

Treat postmortems as letters to future team members held to a consistent quality bar: overloaded teams write subpar postmortems with incomplete action items that make recurrence likely, so prioritize postmortem work, track its completion and review, and give teams adequate time to implement the action plan.

Bootstrap a postmortem culture with a standard template and tooling: a consistent format makes postmortems accessible to outside readers, and tooling that prepopulates incident metadata, stores postmortems in a searchable repository, files action items as tracked bugs whose closure is monitored, and analyzes trends (mean duration, time to detect, time to resolve, blast radius) keeps action items from slipping through the cracks.
Write a postmortem for every significant incident, regardless of whether it triggered a page.
Operate a blameless postmortem culture whose goal is to expose faults and apply engineering fixes rather than to blame or punish individuals.
Keep a documented history of outages and publish and organize postmortems so the whole company can learn, and hold people accountable for following up on the specific actions to prevent recurrence.

Define objective postmortem triggers before incidents occur — such as user-visible downtime beyond a threshold, any data loss, on-call intervention, excessive resolution time, or a monitoring failure — and allow any stakeholder to request a postmortem.

Write postmortems blamelessly: focus on the contributing causes without indicting any individual or team, assuming everyone acted in good faith with the information they had, because a culture of blame drives people to hide issues.
Analyze failures as systemic conditions using blameless postmortems and multi-perspective timelines instead of human-error conclusions.

Give a postmortem the context to be understood beyond the immediate team: explain domain terms in Background and Glossary sections (linking longer docs), present numbers for a consistent impact representation (a well-informed estimate beats none, since you cannot confirm a fix without measuring impact), and identify the root causes and trigger down to lower-level detail.

Document recovery efforts so the postmortem records what happened, how it was mitigated, and how users were impacted, giving the reader a complete view, and give it depth by exploring impact and system flaws across multiple teams and perspectives rather than only the proximate failure, basing every conclusion on linked facts and data.

Use a standard postmortem template that consistently captures the incident root cause and trigger, because doing so enables trend analysis that targets improvements against systemic root-cause types such as faulty software interface design or immature change deployment planning — and prioritize accordingly given that across thousands of Google postmortems (2010-2017) the top outage triggers were binary pushes (37%) and configuration pushes (31%), together about 68%, followed by user-behavior change, processing pipeline, service-provider change, performance decay, capacity management, and hardware, while the top contributing root-cause categories were software (~41%), development-process failure (~20%), complex system behaviors (~17%), deployment planning (~7%), and network failure (~3%).

Postmortems only cover high-impact incidents, so also aggregate alert data systematically to catch frequent low-impact issues and find fixes whose benefit is small per case but large across many events.
A postmortem should capture a summary, user/revenue impact, root causes, trigger, resolution, and detection method for the incident.

Require every postmortem following a user-affecting outage to carry at least one high-priority (P0/P1) bug, because to users a postmortem without subsequent action is indistinguishable from no postmortem at all.

Set an outage policy requiring a postmortem with at least one highest-priority action item addressing the root cause whenever a single incident consumes more than 20% of the four-week error budget, and a highest-priority item on the quarterly planning document whenever a single class of outage consumes more than 20% of the budget over a quarter, and define an escalation policy so that when parties disagree about the error-budget calculation or the actions it requires the issue goes to a designated decision-maker (such as the CTO) to make the call.
Ensure postmortem action items address why a failure happened, not merely roll back the specific change that triggered it.
Postmortem action items should each be typed by intent (for example prevent, mitigate, or process), assigned an owner, and linked to a tracking bug.

Share postmortems as widely as possible (by default company-wide, perhaps with customers) and publish promptly within days while details are fresh, because the value is proportional to the learning created, wider learning reduces repeat incidents, an honest postmortem helps restore shaken trust, and a delayed one loses detail while affected people fill the gap with unfavorable imagination.

Spread postmortem learning through organization-wide announcements, cross-team reviews and reading clubs where one team walks through their incident while others learn, Wheel-of-Misfortune reenactments, and weekly outage reports shared with the widest possible audience.
Treat as operational guidance: Postmortems are essential because, without a formal process to learn from incidents, the same incidents recur indefinitely and can compound or cascade.
Visibly reward people for doing the right thing — a fast rollback or a well-written postmortem — and do not stigmatize individuals or teams who produce postmortems frequently.
Postmortem actions must be owned, prioritized, incremental, and tied to prevention, faster detection, or faster recovery metrics.
Balance postmortem verbosity and readability by abstracting lengthy sources such as chat transcripts and system logs in the main document while linking the unedited versions.

Leave no postmortem unreviewed: have senior engineers assess each draft for completeness — data captured, impact assessed, root cause deep enough, action plan appropriately prioritized, and outcome shared — and store reviewed postmortems in a searchable repository.

When incidents repeat, dig deeper — ask whether action items close too slowly, whether feature velocity is trumping reliability fixes, whether the right action items are captured, whether the service is overdue for a refactor, or whether people are applying Band-Aids to a serious problem — then bring the collaborators from each similar incident together to prevent repeats.

Accept that no service is 100% available and there is no single solution for equalizing and stabilizing network load; keep services reliable with a combination of tools, technologies, and strategies working in harmony, and for most companies use a larger public cloud provider's global load-balancing service rather than building and maintaining your own.

Treat frontend and load-balancer backends as a potentially significant source of load: institute qualification and load-testing to detect frontend degradation from slow or misbehaving backends, and contain one overloading service without harming neighbors by isolating its frontends into a separate pool, enlarging that pool to handle peak, and applying administrative rate limits while it recovers.
Never rely on a single point of failure for large-scale systems; balance load across multiple machines and datacenters.
Remove or modernize technologies that slow flow, create excess support load, or lack cloud-like self-service characteristics.
Use automated resilience, latency, conformity, security, health, and cleanup checks to exercise and maintain cloud systems continuously.

Use DNS-based load balancing as the simplest, most effective way to balance load before a connection even starts, but account for its endemic weakness: it relies on client cooperation to properly expire and refetch DNS records.

Use DNS as the first layer of load balancing, but treat it as insufficient on its own because it gives weak control over client behavior and the recursive-resolver middleman means the authoritative server sees the resolver's address, not the user's.

Use anycast to route clients to the topologically nearest frontend via a single virtual IP for low latency and higher DNS TTL, but mitigate its two issues: too many nearby users can overwhelm a site, and BGP route flaps reset in-progress TCP streams unless stabilized at a connection-level load balancer.
Model load-balancer redundancy as N+1 by spreading packets evenly across a pool of balancer machines (scaling by adding servers) rather than active/passive pairs that give only 1+1 redundancy.
Provision a serving job with N+2 redundancy so it can lose one task to a rolling update and one task to a machine failure simultaneously and still serve peak load.

Terminate TCP and SSL as close to the user as possible in a reverse-proxy front end, then forward to backends over long-lived encrypted connections, and have the front end keep persistent pre-warmed connections to recently active backends so a connection is ready on arrival — minimizing latency, especially the two round trips an HTTPS handshake costs.

Push SSL termination, HTTP request buffering, and low-level attack mitigation (SYN floods) to a high-level Layer 7 edge proxy on a large edge network, because a packet-level IP-layer balancer cannot ameliorate such attacks and terminating/buffering at backend proxies costs two client round trips and can exhaust proxy-tier resources when clients send bytes slowly.

Health-check backends and use a 'lame duck' mode — a backend that fails health checks while still serving in-flight requests — so backends can be gracefully removed or updated without disrupting any user requests.

Give backends an explicit lame-duck state in which a task still serves but asks clients to stop sending new requests, and propagate that state to both active and (via periodic UDP health checks) inactive clients.

Maintain high availability with canarying and gradual rollouts: deploy a new version to a very small number of servers, increase traffic while watching for regressions, let the load balancer route around any instance failing health checks, and administratively remove a regressed instance group without touching the main version.

Use autoscaling (vertical or horizontal) to improve availability and utilization, but configure it carefully because misconfiguration harms the service: autoscale on a load-balancer-observed capacity metric, wait a cool-down for new instances to stabilize before collecting metrics, and combine with autohealing that restarts unhealthy instances so zombie or slow-warming instances do not skew the utilization average.

Make a sharded design resilient to instance failure by replicating each unit of work to a duplicate shard (so the system runs at full speed when one instance fails), placing no two duplicate shards on the same machine, and covering the residual concurrent-double-failure risk with the error budget and log reprocessing.

Build a canary process with three parts — a way to deploy the change to a subset of the population, an evaluation deciding good or bad, and integration of those evaluations into the release process — deploying to a small labeled production segment that receives only a small portion of traffic (split via application versions, load-balancer backend weights, proxy configs, or round-robin DNS), so it demonstrates value by detecting bad candidates with high confidence and identifying good releases without false positives.

Conduct a canary test by upgrading a subset of servers to the new version, incubating ('baking') them for a period, and progressively rolling out only if no unexpected variances occur, reverting the modified servers quickly if anything goes wrong.

Use canary releasing to roll a new version out to a subset of production servers for fast feedback, easy rollback, A/B testing, and low-risk capacity ramp, ensuring any shared resource works with all in-production versions or using a shared-nothing architecture.

Load-test for a wide safety margin while recognizing even generous testing can be exceeded — Niantic load-tested Pokémon GO to five times their most optimistic estimate yet the launch hit nearly fifty times that — so combine load testing with graceful-degradation measures.
Measure load as close to the client as possible, because connections refused at the frontend never reach the backends or inbound-request monitoring, so true client demand is otherwise underestimated.

For stateful systems pinning a session to one backend, do not expect horizontal scaling to relieve overburdened pathways — use intelligent task-level routing such as consistent hashing — and use vertical autoscaling cautiously for short-term hotspots since its uniform growth can make low-traffic instances unnecessarily large.

Configure autoscaling conservatively and asymmetrically: scaling up is more important and less risky than scaling down (failing to scale up causes overload and dropped traffic), so add capacity quickly but reduce it cautiously, keep the service far from key bottlenecks like CPU, and reserve spare capacity for both overload protection and redundancy.

Bound and gate autoscaling: set minimum and maximum instance limits (with quota to reach the max) so a CPU-burning bug or a wedged dependency cannot scale out of control and waste all quota or block the dependency's recovery, and include an easy, obvious, fast, well-documented kill switch and manual override that on-call engineers know how to use.

Provision each component for about 50% CPU at peak as a burst safety margin and autoscale stateless components to avoid static-allocation waste, but keep capacity planning by ensuring quota and setting the maximum instance count high enough to serve peaks yet low enough to limit runaway autoscaling.

Before deploying an autoscaler, do a detailed dependency analysis ensuring backends have spare capacity, degrade gracefully under overload, and that one microservice scaling up will not exhaust shared quota (use limited scaling or per-microservice quotas), and have autoscalers rebalance instances across zones and regions to even out zone sizes and quota usage and diversify failure domains.

As systems grow, combine load balancing, load-based autoscaling, and load shedding (which all serve the same goal and are not independent) deliberately: examine and instrument each new tool's intersection with existing ones, add monitoring to detect feedback loops, and coordinate emergency shutdown triggers across all load-management systems — because tools configured in isolation can form catastrophic feedback loops (a utilization-aware balancer once read load-shed requests as cheaper CPU and sent a failing region more traffic).

Defuse specific load-management feedback loops: set a minimum number of instances per location so autoscaling+load-balancing cannot concentrate all capacity nearest demand and leave no failover spare, and set load-shedding thresholds so the system autoscales before shedding kicks in, otherwise it sheds traffic it could have served by scaling up first.

Use autoscaling for variable and streaming pipelines so you need not provision for peak 100% of the time (it turns down idle workers to avoid paying for unused resources, noting batch pipelines consume all available resources), and plan resources against future-growth estimates — weighing resource cost against efficiency engineering, accounting for hidden costs like storage, cross-region replication, and expensive data stores, and periodically pruning unused data.

Recognize CPU-based autoscaling depends on a strong correlation between CPU usage and useful work: when that correlation breaks (a CPU-hungry daemon or instances burning CPU without working) the autoscaler scales until it exhausts all quota, so limit the maximum instances, restrict daemon CPU, and aggressively throttle a component's CPU as soon as you detect it is doing no useful work.

Set deliberate deadlines on RPC requests — without one a process holds resources for every in-flight request up to a large default, raising latency and risking exhaustion and crashes — having servers terminate over-long requests and clients cancel requests no longer useful to them.

Make criticality a first-class, automatically-propagated property of the RPC system so that outgoing sub-requests inherit their parent's criticality by default, set it as close to the client as possible (e.g., the HTTP frontend), and override it only where it specifically makes sense.
Set an RPC deadline on every request, because no deadline or an excessively high one lets long-past problems keep consuming server resources until a restart.
Do not spend resources on a request whose deadline has already passed — there is no credit for late work — and check the remaining deadline before each stage of multi-stage request processing.

Use deadline propagation: set the deadline high in the stack and pass the remaining absolute deadline down the RPC tree so deep servers immediately abandon already-expired work, reducing it slightly for transit time and considering an upper bound.

Accept that no traffic-management configuration is perfect and works only from a holistic view of system interactions — no amount of load shedding, autoscaling, or throttling saves services that all fail in sync — so plan ahead to fail gracefully with flags, changed defaults, expensive logging, or exposing the parameters the system uses for its decisions.

Apply Non-Abstract Large System Design (NALSD) — capacity planning, component isolation, and graceful degradation — driven through two iterative phases (basic design: Is it possible? Can we do better?; and scaling: Is it feasible? Is it resilient? Can we do better?), bouncing between the questions, restarting when a design flounders, and expressing requirements as SLOs so each iteration is compared against a goal and error budget.

Keep large-system design 'non-abstract' by turning the whiteboard into concrete resource estimates at multiple steps (all systems eventually run on real computers, networks, and datacenters), using rounded-up assumptions and scientific notation to avoid prematurely hitting limits and unit-mismatch errors, since sound reasoning with reasonable assumptions matters more than perfect final numbers and reduces last-minute changes for physical constraints.

Evaluate every design iteration with the four NALSD questions — Is it possible (buildable without 'magic')? Can we do better (as simple as reasonably possible)? Is it feasible (fits budget and time)? Is it resilient (survives inevitable disruptions)? — and treat NALSD as a learned skill needing regular practice.

Start a system design from the simplest possible point — a single machine — and evaluate it (even an infeasible single-machine design teaches you how to reason about constraints), then test the design by asking what happens when each component fails, since a single machine has many single points of failure (CPU, memory, storage, power, network, cooling) and cannot support meaningful SLOs.
Use stress tests to find the limits of a system and its components, because many components do not degrade gracefully beyond a point but instead fail catastrophically.

Build an appropriate indexed data structure as data arrives so lookups stay fast at scale rather than scanning raw logs per query, identify the binding constraint rather than only total capacity (a machine may hold 100 TB yet be limited to ~200 IOPS on an HDD, so choose media meeting the IO requirement not just the size), and when joining data sets of very different sizes, scale the larger one by building an on-demand lookup store keyed for the bigger input and looping only over the smaller stream.

Know the limits of MapReduce-style batch processing: it scales horizontally so adding machines always lets it complete without exhausting disk or RAM, but it cannot meet a low data-freshness SLO, and its arbitrary non-overlapping batches cannot join records spanning batches (a query in one batch and its click in the next never join).
When joining streams where one side may lag, set aside an unmatched record and retry up to a time limit, then discard it if still unmatched by that limit.

Get past a single machine's IO limits by sharding inputs and outputs across instances by hashing a key modulo the shard count, sharding each component by the key it is read and written by so every component shares a consistent view of the data.

Shard data so that N tasks run in parallel, each copying and verifying one Nth of the data, which requires schema and deployment design that balances data, ensures shard independence, and avoids contention, and can cut restore wall time by orders of magnitude.

Prefer scaling horizontally — many instances each receiving an evenly distributed trickle of load — over scaling vertically with more CPU and RAM per machine, and separate software components by how you expect the system to grow so parts scale independently with no part bound to a single piece of hardware or software instance.

Recognize for operational decisions: In the ideal case load is spread so every backend consumes the same CPU; because you can only send traffic until the most-loaded task reaches capacity, a large load spread wastes the reserved-but-unused capacity of every other task.

Treat a single datacenter as a single point of failure: duplicate data across geographically separate datacenters so a multi-day power or network outage in one can fail over to another, and replicate state without multiplying compute by solving the consensus problem — three or five replicas using an algorithm such as Paxos — accepting at least one inter-node round trip per write (which bounds sequential throughput) while parallelizing writes where possible.
Prefer a distributed master-worker build cluster over a single standalone server, which is a single point of failure that cannot handle larger workloads.

Decide replica locations by trading off failure-domain coverage against latency, because spreading replicas farther apart tolerates larger failures but increases round-trip time and operation latency.

Do not host a critical periodic-scheduling service on a single machine; decouple processes from machines via a reliable datacenter scheduler and place replicas in diverse locations so a single power-distribution failure cannot take out the whole service.
Keep base services such as cron with very few dependencies so they continue to function even when parts of the datacenter fail.
Run multiple replicas of a distributed scheduler with Paxos for consistent state, designating a single leader as the only replica that may modify shared state and launch jobs.

Treat data processing as business-critical (delayed or incorrect pipeline data becomes expensive, labor-intensive user-facing issues) and involve SREs from the early design stages so the pipeline can be easily released, modified, and run without harming customers, using an ETL model — extract, transform (reformat, aggregate, index), load into a specialized format — to prepare data efficiently.

Treat stale data as almost always better than incorrect data: design the pipeline so delayed input causes it to stall, wait, and resume once data is available — keeping quality high rather than propagating incomplete or corrupt data — and create data dependencies respected by all stages, exploiting that streaming with event-time processing lets a downstream stage start as soon as the corresponding upstream portion completes, unlike batch where each stage waits for its predecessor to finish entirely.

Give each ETL or pipeline component a single responsibility (easier to develop, test, and operate) and isolate independent data streams such as different event types so they cannot impact one another, while requiring each data type or stream to be explicitly enabled with explicit ownership, since holding producing teams accountable yields higher data quality and a clear communication channel during incidents.

Define and measure SLOs for a data pipeline to automatically detect when it is unhealthy and to be notified before exceeding the error budget: data-freshness SLOs typically take one of three forms (X% processed within Y, oldest data no older than Y, or job completed within Y), and create data-correctness SLOs — generating 'golden data' via test accounts when there is no predefined correct output — to alert on discrepancies between expected and actual output.

Honor data priority and measure end-to-end: when promising a tighter SLO on high-priority data, process it before lower-priority data under resource constraints (separate priority queues or jobs, retrying lower-worker failures on higher-provisioned workers), and measure pipeline SLOs end-to-end rather than per-stage, since per-stage success can mask a corruption bug where one stage adds a field a downstream stage drops.

Canary the entire pipeline, not a single process: process the same real production data as the live pipeline but skip writes to production storage (e.g. two-phase mutation) and compare canary versus live results for data differences, and for replicated/multihomed pipelines that cannot canary per region, roll out a small percentage of data first or in dry-run mode.

Optimize a pipeline only for the features it actually needs (e.g. you do not need 'exactly once' if work units are idempotent), and use the idempotent-mutation pattern so repeated executions on the same input always produce the same result and reprocessing after failure stores no duplicates or errors.
